{{short description|Japanese chemist and pharmacologist}}
{{nihongo|'''Hachiro Sugimoto'''|杉本 八郎|Sugimoto Hachirō}} is a Japanese [[chemist]] and [[pharmacologist]], known for his discovery of [[Donepezil]].

==Research==
Sugimoto's research on E2020 (now called ''Donepezil''), an [[acetylcholinesterase]] inhibitor, first began at Eisai's Tsukuba Research Laboratories in 1983,<ref>Sugimoto, Hachiro; Ogura, Hiroo; Arai, Yasuo; Iimura, Youichi; Yamanishi, Yoshiharu (25 January 2002), "Research and Development of Donepezil Hydrochloride, a New Type of Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitor", ''The Japanese Journal of Pharmacology'' (2002) '''89''' (1): 7–20</ref> because his mother suffered from [[dementia]].<ref name="eisai">[http://www.eisai.com/company/profile/history/products/aricept/index.html Alzheimer's Disease Treatment The Aricept R&D Story | Eisai Co., Ltd.]</ref> At that time, there was a hypothesis suggested that [[acetylcholine]]s were closely linked to abnormal decreases in memory function in patients with [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref name="eisai"/> His research group was finally able to successfully create Donepezil with a promising enough profile for the compound to become a drug candidate.<ref name="eisai"/>

==Biography==
Sugimoto was born as the eighth child among nine children in a downtown section of Tokyo in 1943, and joined [[Eisai (company)|Eisai]], a Japanese pharmaceutical company.<ref name="yomi">[http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/adv/chuo/dy/people/20100819.htm Developed the magic bullet for Alzheimer's disease after overcoming many difficulties : People : Chuo Online : Yomiuri Online]</ref> While working for Eisai, he graduated from [[Chuo University]] in 1969 and obtained his doctorate in [[pharmacology]] at [[Hiroshima University]] in 2002.<ref name="yomi"/> In 2003, he retired from Eisai, and became Professor in the Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, [[Kyoto University]].<ref name="yomi"/>

==Recognition==
For his achievement, Sugimoto received the Award of Science from Eisai in October 1993, the Award of Engineering from the Pharmaceutical Society of Japan in March 1998, the Special Galien Prize in the UK in April 1998, the Chemistry-Bio Tsukuba Award in May 1998, and the Imperial Award for Invention in June 2002<ref name="yomi"/>
